title: Is this a rhetorical question? | RHETORIC & LITERARY DEVICES

entries.note: Came to English in the Renaissance; a comparison using like or as, taught at school through its link with similar.
From Greek [[from:metaphora]], a transfer or carrying over, because it carries one meaning to another by saying a thing is another thing.
Means bad expression or bad speech, applicable to any poor speaking but nowadays usually applied to mixed metaphors.
A merging of two commonly used idioms or metaphors, as in [[see:we'll burn that bridge when we come to it]].

entries.term: we'll burn that bridge when we come to it
entries.note: An example of mixed idioms, or a [[see:malaphor]].
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode on corporate jargon, alongside [[see:opening the kimono]].
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode on corporate jargon.
A big literary device Britons pride themselves on, broken down into [[see:verbal irony]], [[see:situational irony]] and [[see:dramatic irony]].
A form of irony; specifically [[see:verbal irony]], like saying you're excited to pay your mortgage.
Includes [[see:sarcasm]] and ironic similes like [[see:as clear as mud]], but needn't be self-aware, like angrily yelling that you're not angry.
An oxymoronic, sarcastic simile given as an example of [[see:verbal irony]].
A reversal of expectations, often in plays, illustrated by [[see:Romeo and Juliet]] and [[see:The Wizard of Oz]].
Alanis Morissette's song, whose supposed situational ironies the hosts doubt, joking that its real irony is claiming to demonstrate irony.
Applied jokingly to the song [[see:Ironic]], which fails to be ironic.
Irony where the audience knows the full implications of a character's actions, as with Iago's scheme in [[see:Othello]] or Duncan's trust in [[see:Macbeth]].
Romeo's poisoning himself to join a Juliet who isn't dead is both situational and dramatic irony.
Iago tells the audience his scheme while Othello doesn't know, so Othello's actions are [[see:dramatic irony]].
Duncan's praise of Macbeth is dramatic irony, while the witches' prophecy unfolding unexpectedly adds situational irony.
Full of [[see:situational irony]]: Dorothy's companions already have the qualities they seek from the Wizard.
A brief paradox of contradictory words; itself an oxymoron meaning sharp-dull or clever-stupid, its oxy- shared with [[same-root:oxygen]] and [[same-root:acute]].
An ostensibly self-contradictory scenario; from Greek [[from:paradoxa]], contrary to opinion.
A classic [[see:oxymoron]] whose words contradict each other without context.
A classic [[see:oxymoron]] whose words contradict each other without context.
In a sense an [[see:oxymoron]] that still makes perfect sense.
Literally one by means of two: two words joined by and to express one idea, like [[see:nice and warm]] for nicely warm.
A legal [[see:hendiadys]] that annoyed an Australian lawyer, since the law doesn't treat ceasing and desisting separately.
A stock legal [[see:hendiadys]] covering all bases while focusing on one thing.
A [[see:hendiadys]] meaning nicely cozy.
The OED's example of [[see:hendiadys]], instead of nicely warm.
The sharp or acid generator, sharing its oxy- with [[same-root:oxymoron]].
As in acute angle, a relative of the oxy- in [[same-root:oxymoron]].
A joke [[see:oxymoron]] poking fun at the idea.
A joke [[see:oxymoron]] attributed to [[see:George Carlin]].
Often misexplained as a question needing no answer; really a question asked for the sake of rhetoric, like [[see:are you not entertained]].
A [[see:rhetorical question]] from the film Gladiator.
Old English poetry's main device before rhyme arrived from French; ad- plus letter, stressing the repeated letter.
A rhyme form with an odd scheme, famously introduced by [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]].
Its opening, read by Rob, is littered with [[see:alliteration]]; the hosts joke about having a special Beowulf voice.
Jess recites its bouncy rhyming opening to show [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s use of rhyme.
A French term for a rhyme of just one syllable at a line's end, contrasted with [[see:rime riche]].
A French term for a prized rhyme of three syllables at a line's end, contrasted with [[see:rime pauvre]].
A sub-type of [[see:alliteration]]: the repetition of vowel sounds.
Repetition of s sounds, present in the Beowulf passage; a sub-form of [[see:consonance]].
Named as the broader category of which [[see:sibilance]] is a sub-form.
A big simile or metaphor, a thought with another thought's hat on; from Greek [[from:analogia]], proportion or correspondence.
An even bigger comparison, a whole story standing for something else, classically [[see:The Pilgrim's Progress]].
John Bunyan's classic [[see:allegory]], a journey standing for life, its Valley of the Shadow of Death for experiencing death.

entries.term: a rose by any other name would smell as sweet
entries.note: An example of a smaller [[see:analogy]], from [[see:Romeo and Juliet]].
A form of [[see:hyperbaton]] moving one word, Yoda-style; Greek for turning upside down, remembered via astronomy and Yoda.
Unusual word order for emphasis or meter, as in [[see:to be or not to be, that is the question]]; means stepping over or beyond.

entries.term: to be or not to be, that is the question
entries.note: The iconic [[see:hyperbaton]], from Hamlet's soliloquy, instead of the question is to be or not to be.
Repeating the same words at the start of consecutive lines, as in [[see:I Have a Dream]]; meaning carrying back.
Repeating the same words at the end of consecutive lines, as in the [[see:Gettysburg Address]].
Martin Luther King's speech, with repeated I have a dream and Let freedom ring, exemplifies [[see:anaphora]].
Abraham Lincoln's of the people, by the people, for the people exemplifies [[see:epistrophe]].
Using [[see:anaphora]] and [[see:epistrophe]] together, as in [[see:for want of a nail]].
An example of [[see:symploce]], with for want of a as anaphora and was lost as epistrophe.
Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next, as in Yoda's fear leads to anger; meaning a doubling back.
Means turning about: repeating a phrase in reverse order, as in [[see:ask not what your country can do for you]].

entries.term: ask not what your country can do for you
entries.note: John F. Kennedy's line, an example of [[see:antimetabole]].
Means unconnected: omitting conjunctions, as in [[see:I came, I saw, I conquered]].
Means many connections: adding extra conjunctions, as in James Joyce's we lived and laughed and loved and left.

entries.term: I came, I saw, I conquered
entries.note: The iconic example of [[see:asyndeton]].
Greek for plainness or simplicity; negating the opposite for emphasis, as in Beowulf's not unfamiliar with hardship.
Ramming a word inside another, as in [[see:unflippingbelievable]], [[see:fan-bloody-tastic]] or [[see:a whole nother]].
Jess's favourite example of [[see:tmesis]].
Rob's example of [[see:tmesis]], which he thought a bit near the knuckle.
A common [[see:tmesis]] that annoys Rob, also a case of [[see:rebracketing]].
Something put in the middle of a word; the F-word and bloody can arguably be used as infixes.
Discussed in an earlier episode.
Substituting a related term, like [[see:the White House]] for the US government or [[see:Houston]] for NASA; it came up in a previous episode.
Using a part for the whole, like [[see:under my roof]] for one's house or [[see:hand]] for a worker.
Used for the US government, an example of [[see:metonymy]].
Astronauts' name for NASA, an example of [[see:metonymy]].
Roof standing for the whole house, an example of [[see:synecdoche]].
A worker called a hand, as in stable hand or all hands on deck, is [[see:synecdoche]].
Wimbledon's postcode, used by sports writers to avoid repetition, an example of [[see:metonymy]].
Meaning alphabetical, also a Latin word; an elaborate [[see:acrostic]] where each line or stanza begins with the next letter, like [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s poem ABC.
An [[see:abecedarius]] is described as a more elaborate acrostic poem.
One word governing several parts differently, as in she broke his car and his heart, or Pope's Rape of the Lock; from a root meaning to yoke.
Immediate repetition of a word for emphasis, like King Lear's never, never; shares a Greek root meaning to yoke with [[same-root:zeugma]].
Means against expectation: a sentence whose ending changes the meaning of its start, often attributed to Groucho Marx; related to [[see:garden path sentence]]s.

entries.term: I've had a perfectly wonderful evening, but this wasn't it
entries.note: A [[see:paraprosdokian]] commonly attributed to Groucho Marx.
An example of the sexist marriage-joke [[see:paraprosdokian]], which the hosts find outdated.

entries.term: marriage is a great institution, but I'm not ready for an institution
entries.note: A Mae West [[see:paraprosdokian]] that Jess links to [[see:zeugma]].
A sentence you must reinterpret, like [[see:the old man the boat]]; like a [[see:paraprosdokian]] but less funny, and discussed before.
An example of a [[see:garden path sentence]].

entries.term: the florist sent the flowers was pleased
entries.note: An example of a [[see:garden path sentence]].
